You pass with a stack that checks all three failures. Counting each kind of bracket instead of using a stack answers true for

A stack and a queue are the two disciplines for the order work comes back out. A stack is last in, first out: whatever you pushed most recently is the only thing you can read or remove. A queue is first in, first out: whatever you pushed longest ago is the one that comes out next. In C++ both are adaptors in the sense that matters for an interview: the operations they allow, not the container underneath, are the whole point.

The shape of problem that signals a stack is anything with a most-recent-first cancellation: matching brackets or tags, undoing the last edit, walking a tree or graph depth-first, or evaluating an expression where an operator needs its two most recent operands. A queue is signalled by fairness or arrival order: handling messages or commands in the order they arrived, or a breadth-first search, where the next node to visit is the oldest one still waiting.
The mechanism, in C++, is choosing the container the discipline actually needs. A
is a stack with everything O(1), amortised for the push, and it is the default: reach for
only when the type itself must forbid indexing or iterating. A queue needs O(1) removal from the front, which a vector doesn't give, so

, and a fixed-size queue in a loop that must not allocate is a ring buffer instead. The same discipline, kept under an extra invariant, gives a monotonic stack, one that never lets a smaller element sit above a larger one, answering "next larger element" style questions in one pass.
What trips people up under pressure is popping past empty: reading
on an empty container is undefined behaviour that a plain build won't flag, so the fix is checking

from your own pop. The other is treating "amortised O(1)" as "O(1) every time": a structure such as a two-stack queue moves every element exactly once over its whole life, but one particular call can still move all of them at once, which a real-time loop with a deadline can't absorb.

You meet this in the interview question itself: check whether a string's brackets are balanced, which is a stack problem the moment you notice that the bracket due to close next is always the one that opened most recently.

Stacks answer "the most recent one first": the bracket to close next, the last edit to undo, the next node of a depth-first search, and the pending operands when you evaluate an expression. Queues answer "the oldest one first": the next node of a breadth-first search, and messages or commands handled in the order they arrived.
